the IEEE 34 node test feeder is a good benchmark to validate distribution system analysis software.
the IEEE 34 node test feeder data can be simplified to a balanced three phase system without significant errors in the voltage profile and system losses.

a comparative study of the IEEE 14 node test feeder under practical simplifications, such as balanced three phase feeder and spot loads.
a comparative study of a simplified balanced IEEE 34 node test feeder with a practical IEEE 34 node feeder.
the comparison of voltage profiles and power losses of a balanced three phase system with the IEEE node test system.

the simplified three phase balanced feeder model is adequate for most practical applications in distribution planning and operation.

the IEEE 34 node test feeder is a valuable tool in the analysis of distribution systems and the simplifying assumptions used in the analysis of the IEEE 32 node feeder can be used with confidence in the analysis of practical distribution systems.

the use of a simplified balanced three phase feeder is justified when the objective is to size equipment and determine control parameters for the distribution system.
, the simplified three phase system with spot loads, is an adequate model for distribution system planning and operations.
a three phase system with a single phase lateral and spot loads is adequate for distribution system analysis and design.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the IEEE 34 node test feeder can be used for planning and control of distribution systems under simplifying assumptions.
the simplified balanced three phase feeder is a good starting point for the analysis of the distribution system, with the exact IEEE test feeder used for the final validation.

, the simplifying assumptions do not affect the results in the planning phase, where system losses and voltages at all nodes are not of interest, but in the operating phase, where the voltage profile is important, the simplification can lead to significant differences in the system voltages and the corresponding control actions required to maintain the voltages within the limits.
